Clinical Reference

Sepsis & Septic Shock v2

On this page
Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection (Sepsis-3). Septic shock = the sub-set needing vasopressors for MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids.
Organ dysfunction = acute SOFA ↑ ≥2 Antibiotics within 1 hour 30 mL/kg crystalloid if hypotensive or lactate ≥4 Septic shock mortality >40% Norepinephrine first-line pressor
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story from microbe to shock

Sepsis is not the infection itself — it is the host's own response gone haywire. The steps are worth learning in order, because every therapy interrupts one specific step.

  1. Pathogen recognition. Microbial PAMPs (pathogen-associated molecular patterns — LPS/endotoxin, peptidoglycan, flagellin) and host DAMPs (released by injured cells) bind pattern-recognition receptors, especially Toll-like receptors (TLRs) on macrophages and neutrophils.
  2. Cytokine storm. TLR ligation activates NF-κB, unleashing TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 (plus IL-8, etc.). An appropriate local response becomes systemic and dysregulated.
  3. Endothelial injury & glycocalyx shedding. Cytokines strip the protective endothelial glycocalyx and open inter-cellular junctions → capillary leak → plasma pours into the interstitium (absolute and relative hypovolemia, edema).
  4. Vasodilation. Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) floods the vessel wall with nitric oxide → arterial and venous dilation and catecholamine hypo-responsiveness → distributive shock.
  5. Microvascular thrombosis / DIC. Tissue-factor expression plus consumed protein C and antithrombin drive microthrombi and consumptive coagulopathy, starving tissue beds even where flow looks adequate.
  6. Mitochondrial dysfunction ("cytopathic hypoxia"). Even after oxygen delivery is restored, mitochondria cannot use it → cellular energy failure.
  7. Neuroendocrine failure. Relative adrenal insufficiency (CIRCI) and vasopressin depletion (an early surge exhausts neurohypophyseal stores) rob the vasculature of its backup tone systems.
Picture the circulation as a garden-hose network feeding a house. The infection is a fire. The body's alarm accidentally slits every hose (capillary leak — water sprays out) and relaxes every hose wall at once (vasodilation — pressure collapses). To keep water reaching every faucet (organ) you must put out the fire (antibiotics + source control), refill the system (fluids), squeeze the hose walls back to tension (norepinephrine ± vasopressin), and if the pump itself is weak (septic cardiomyopathy) add a booster pump (dobutamine). Steroids re-tighten the loose fittings so the squeezing actually holds.
The cascade, and where therapy lands: antibiotics/source control cut the top box; fluids refill the leak (left); norepinephrine/vasopressin oppose vasodilation (right); steroids restore vascular tone at the bottom; dobutamine supports the pump when septic cardiomyopathy coexists.
Cytokine release & immune signalling — the "storm" that injures the endothelium.
Lu L, Zhang H, Zhan M, et al. — Frontiers in Cell & Developmental Biology (Fcell-08-00677-g001), Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.
The trigger: bacterial pathogens (Gram stain). Identifying the organism drives antibiotic de-escalation.
CDC / Dr. Holdeman — Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

Two phases, not one. The early hyperinflammatory "cytokine storm" is quickly counter-regulated by a compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome (CARS): lymphocyte apoptosis, monocyte deactivation, and immune exhaustion. This is why many patients who survive the initial insult die later of secondary/nosocomial infections and persistent organ dysfunction — and why blanket anti-inflammatory "magic bullets" (anti-TNF, high-dose steroids, activated protein C) have repeatedly failed: the immune state is a moving target, inflamed in one compartment and paralysed in another.

The through-line of this whole guide: antibiotics remove the PAMP source (the only truly disease-modifying step); crystalloid replaces preload lost to capillary leak; norepinephrine restores α1 tone against NO-driven vasodilation; vasopressin works through V1 receptors when catecholamine receptors are down-regulated; hydrocortisone treats CIRCI and re-sensitizes the vasculature to catecholamines; dobutamine adds β1 inotropy for sepsis-induced myocardial depression.

🩸

Lactate & perfusion — the number you will chase

Lactate is the single most useful resuscitation biomarker in sepsis, but only if you understand why it moves. Under normal aerobic conditions, pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is fully oxidised. When oxygen delivery fails to meet demand — or when mitochondria cannot use the oxygen delivered (cytopathic hypoxia) — pyruvate is shunted to lactate by anaerobic glycolysis. The liver normally clears lactate back to glucose via the Cori cycle; in sepsis, hepatic hypoperfusion and dysfunction reduce that clearance, so lactate accumulates from both increased production and decreased clearance.

LactateMeaningAction
> 2 mmol/LAbnormal; tissue hypoperfusion; a criterion for septic shock (with pressor need).Resuscitate; remeasure in 2–4 h.
≥ 4 mmol/LSevere illness; "cryptic shock" even if normotensive.Triggers 30 mL/kg crystalloid in the SSC/SEP-1 bundle.
Clearance ≥ 10–20% / 2 hResuscitation is working.Continue; a reasonable perfusion target (SSC 2021).
Don't be fooledLactate also rises from β2-adrenergic stimulation (endogenous catecholamines, epinephrine/albuterol infusions), seizures, regional ischemia (bowel/limb), thiamine deficiency, metformin, and impaired hepatic clearance (cirrhosis). A high lactate that is falling on serial checks is reassuring; a normal lactate does not exclude sepsis. Pair it with a bedside perfusion marker — capillary refill time — which ANDROMEDA-SHOCK validated as a resuscitation target.
Below a critical oxygen-delivery threshold, oxygen consumption becomes supply-dependent and lactate climbs — the physiologic basis for resuscitating to restore perfusion and clear lactate.
The Cori cycle — muscle lactate is returned to the liver and reconverted to glucose. Hepatic hypoperfusion in sepsis blunts this clearance, compounding lactic acidosis.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)

Workup

What to order & when — and how to read it

🧪

Sepsis work-up order set

Serum lactateDraw immediately. Repeat within 2–4 h if >2 to track clearance. Marker of hypoperfusion/anaerobic metabolism (also β-adrenergic driven).STAT
Blood cultures ×2 setsAerobic + anaerobic, from 2 sites, before antibiotics — but never delay antibiotics to obtain them. Add line cultures if CLABSI suspected.Before abx
CBC + differentialLeukocytosis, leukopenia, bandemia, thrombocytopenia (coag SOFA input, early DIC).Initial
CMPCreatinine/BUN (renal SOFA), electrolytes, bicarbonate/anion gap, LFTs + bilirubin (liver SOFA).Initial
Coags: PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimerIf bleeding, thrombocytopenia, or DIC suspected.If indicated
ProcalcitoninDo NOT use to decide whether to start antibiotics. Useful for stopping/de-escalating with clinical judgment. Falsely low early/localized; falsely high post-surgery, trauma, cardiogenic shock, ESRD.Stewardship
Source imagingCXR (pneumonia); CT abd/pelvis (intra-abdominal/abscess); renal US/CT (obstructive uropathy); soft-tissue imaging (necrotizing infection); LP (meningitis); echo (endocarditis).Find the source
ABG/VBG + glucoseAcid-base status, oxygenation; central venous O₂ where available.Initial
Urinalysis + urine cultureUrosepsis is a leading source, especially in elderly/instrumented patients.Initial

How to read the key abnormal labs

LabDirection in sepsisMechanism / confounders
Lactate↑ (>2, severe ≥4)Tissue hypoperfusion + anaerobic glycolysis; also raised by β2-agonists/epinephrine, seizures, and impaired hepatic clearance (cirrhosis) — interpret the trend.
WBC↑ or ↓Demargination/marrow release (↑) vs consumption/marrow suppression (↓, worse prognosis); bands reflect left shift. Steroids raise WBC independently.
Platelets↓Consumption in DIC, marrow suppression, sequestration — coagulation SOFA input.
Creatinine↑Hypoperfusion + acute tubular injury; may lag hours behind true GFR fall (falsely reassuring early).
Bilirubin↑Sepsis-associated cholestasis / hypoperfusion — liver SOFA input.
Bicarbonate / anion gap↓ HCO₃ / ↑ gapLactic (high-gap) acidosis; a normal-gap acidosis can appear from large-volume 0.9% saline (hyperchloremic).
Procalcitonin↑ (bacterial)Rises 6–12 h into bacterial infection; low in viral/localized; high in surgery/trauma/ESRD regardless of infection.

Key imaging findings

Study (when ordered)FindingWhat it changes
CXR (respiratory symptoms / hypoxia)Focal consolidation; bilateral infiltrates (ARDS)Confirms pulmonary source; guides CAP vs HAP coverage; ARDS → lung-protective vent.
CT abdomen/pelvis (abdominal pain, ↑LFTs, unknown source)Abscess, perforation, obstruction, gasTriggers source control (drain/surgery) — antibiotics alone will fail.
Renal/bladder US or CT (flank pain, obstructive labs)Hydronephrosis, stone, pyonephrosisEmergent decompression (stent/nephrostomy) for obstructed infected system.
Soft-tissue CT/MRI (pain out of proportion, crepitus)Gas, fascial edema/enhancementNecrotizing infection → emergent surgical debridement — do not wait for imaging if clinically obvious.

Treat

Initial resuscitation — the "Hour-1" bundle

⏱️

Do these the moment sepsis is recognized

SSC 2021
1
Measure lactate + draw cultures; give broad-spectrum antibiotics ≤1 h
The single most life-saving step
▾
Antibiotics remove the PAMP source driving the entire cascade. Each hour of delay after hypotension in septic shock adds ~7.6% to mortality (Kumar 2006). Target within 1 hour for septic shock and probable sepsis; for possible sepsis without shock, a rapid investigation window up to 3 h is acceptable while you assess.

Empiric choice depends on source and MRSA/Pseudomonas risk — see the full antibiotic ladder in the Wards tab. Draw 2 sets of blood cultures first unless that would delay antibiotics.

2
30 mL/kg IV balanced crystalloid
If hypotensive OR lactate ≥4 mmol/L
▾
Restores preload lost to capillary leak and venodilation. Start immediately, complete within 3 h. Balanced crystalloid (LR / Plasma-Lyte) is preferred over 0.9% saline (SMART trial sepsis subgroup — lower mortality; saline causes hyperchloremic acidosis).

In CHF/ESRD, still give the initial bolus but in smaller aliquots (250–500 mL) with frequent reassessment (see comorbidity table, Wards tab).

3
Vasopressors for MAP ≥65 if still hypotensive
During or after fluids — don't wait to finish all fluid
▾
Norepinephrine is first-line (α1 vasoconstriction against NO-driven vasodilation). Can be started through a good peripheral IV briefly to avoid delay while central access is obtained (CLOVERS supports early pressors). Full dosing in the ICU tab.

Then reassess volume status and perfusion (dynamic measures, not CVP) and remeasure lactate if the first was >2.

CMS SEP-1The regulatory bundle mirrors this in a 3-hour (lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg if hypotensive or lactate ≥4) and 6-hour (repeat lactate, vasopressors for fluid-refractory hypotension, documented perfusion reassessment) structure.

The first 3 hours — a practical timeline

TimeDo
0 minRecognize (screen + clinical gestalt); IV access ×2; send lactate, cultures ×2, CBC, CMP, coags, VBG.
< 60 minBroad-spectrum antibiotics matched to source; start 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid if hypotensive or lactate ≥4.
1–3 hComplete fluids; start norepinephrine if MAP <65 during/after fluids; arrange source imaging/control; call the appropriate consult.
2–4 hRepeat lactate; reassess perfusion (MAP, cap refill, urine output, mentation) with dynamic measures; decide disposition (floor vs ICU).
Prevent

Prevention & USPSTF-relevant screening

🛡️

Reduce sepsis before it starts

There is no "sepsis screening test" for asymptomatic adults — prevention is vaccination, infection control, and comorbidity optimization. Relevant USPSTF Grade A/B and CDC/ACIP items:

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BScreen for bacteriuria with urine culturePregnant persons (asymptomatic bacteriuria → prevents pyelonephritis/urosepsis)
BScreen & treat latent TBAdults at increased risk (prevents reactivation/dissemination)
AHIV screeningAdolescents/adults 15–65 (immunosuppression → invasive infection risk)
BPrediabetes/T2DM screeningAdults 35–70 with overweight/obesity (diabetes ↑ infection severity)

Vaccination (ACIP) — the highest-yield sepsis prevention

  • Pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15→PPSV23): all adults ≥65 and younger adults with risk conditions — prevents pneumococcal pneumonia/bacteremia.
  • Influenza annually — post-influenza bacterial pneumonia (incl. MRSA) is a major sepsis driver.
  • COVID-19, RSV (≥60/75), Hib & meningococcal for asplenia/complement deficiency (encapsulated-organism sepsis).
  • Asplenia counseling: vaccinate against encapsulated organisms + carry emergency antibiotics — overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is fulminant.
The best outpatient sepsis intervention is early recognition: teach at-risk patients (diabetes, immunosuppression, indwelling devices) to seek care for fever + confusion/rigors rather than "waiting it out."
Escalate

When it can't stay in clinic

🚑

Immediate ED / admission triggers

Any suspected sepsis with hypotension, lactate ≥4, altered mentation, or a hard red flag → activate the ED sepsis pathway now: IV access, labs + cultures + lactate, antibiotics ≤1 h, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, and continuous monitoring. Outpatient oral antibiotics are not appropriate for sepsis with organ dysfunction.
Admit for sepsis (organ dysfunction) even without shock; go straight to ICU/step-down for vasopressor need, lactate ≥4, respiratory failure, or rapidly progressive organ dysfunction.
🛏️ Wards — antibiotics, source control, daily trending
Admit

Who to admit & where

📋

Admission triage

  • Floor: sepsis (organ dysfunction) that is stabilizing after initial resuscitation, with a clear source, no vasopressor need, and a reassuring lactate trend.
  • Step-down / ICU: septic shock (any vasopressor), lactate ≥4, respiratory failure, rapidly progressive organ dysfunction, or high illness-severity scores.
Trajectory beats a single snapshot. A normotensive patient whose lactate is rising or whose work of breathing is climbing is heading for the unit — escalate before the crash.

Treat

Empiric antibiotics — full ladders

💊

Choose by source, then de-escalate at 48–72 h

verify renal dose + local antibiogram

Principles: broad early, cover the likely source + local resistance, add MRSA coverage for risk factors, add antipseudomonal coverage for hospital-acquired/neutropenic/severe disease. Narrow within 48–72 h on cultures. Typical duration 7 days with source control (SSC 2021 favors shorter courses); longer for undrained focus, endocarditis, S. aureus bacteremia, osteomyelitis, or immunocompromise.

Backbone agents — dose ladder (normal renal function)

DrugStart / loadTitrationTarget / maxWhy it worksIf allergic / alt
Piperacillin-tazobactam4.5 g IVq8h → q6h; extended infusion over 4 h4.5 g q6hAntipseudomonal β-lactam + β-lactamase inhibitor; broad Gram-neg + anaerobe cover.Cefepime + metronidazole; carbapenem (penicillin-allergic → cephalosporin usually safe if non-anaphylactic).
Cefepime2 g IV q8h—2 g q8h (max)4th-gen cephalosporin; antipseudomonal, less AKI with vancomycin than pip-tazo.Aztreonam (true β-lactam allergy) + metronidazole.
Meropenem1 g IV q8h→ 2 g q8h for CNS / highly resistant organisms2 g q8hCarbapenem — broadest Gram-neg incl. ESBL; anaerobe cover.Reserve; cross-reactivity with penicillin low (<1%).
Ceftriaxone2 g IV daily—2 g daily (q12h for meningitis)3rd-gen cephalosporin; CAP, urosepsis, meningitis backbone (not antipseudomonal).Aztreonam or fluoroquinolone.
Vancomycin (MRSA)Load 25–30 mg/kg IVthen 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h, adjust to AUC/troughAUC 400–600Glycopeptide — Gram-positive incl. MRSA; the loading dose gets you to target fast in shock.Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h; daptomycin 6–10 mg/kg IV daily (not for pneumonia — surfactant inactivates it).
Metronidazole500 mg IV q8h—500 mg q8hAnaerobic cover when the backbone lacks it (e.g. with cefepime/ceftriaxone).Built-in with pip-tazo/carbapenem (omit).
Clindamycin (add-on)900 mg IV q8h—900 mg q8hAnti-toxin (ribosomal) effect in necrotizing/toxic-shock strep & staph.Linezolid (also suppresses toxin).

Empiric regimen by suspected source

SourceRegimen (representative)
Severe CAPCeftriaxone 2 g IV daily + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily (or levofloxacin 750 mg). Add vancomycin/linezolid if MRSA risk; antipseudomonal β-lactam if Pseudomonas risk (ATS/IDSA CAP 2019).
HAP / VAPAntipseudomonal β-lactam (pip-tazo 4.5 g q6h, cefepime 2 g q8h, or meropenem 1 g q8h) + vancomycin/linezolid; second antipseudomonal agent if high resistance risk.
Urinary / urosepsisCeftriaxone 2 g daily; escalate to cefepime/pip-tazo/carbapenem if healthcare-associated or prior resistant GNR. Relieve obstruction urgently.
Intra-abdominalPip-tazo 4.5 g q6–8h or (cefepime 2 g q8h + metronidazole 500 mg q8h) or meropenem 1 g q8h. Source control (drain/surgery).
Skin / soft tissueNon-purulent: cefazolin/ceftriaxone. Purulent/MRSA risk: add vancomycin/linezolid. Necrotizing fasciitis: pip-tazo or carbapenem + vancomycin + clindamycin 900 mg q8h + emergent debridement.
Unknown sourceVancomycin + antipseudomonal β-lactam (pip-tazo 4.5 g q6–8h, cefepime 2 g q8h, or meropenem 1 g q8h).
Febrile neutropeniaAntipseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy (cefepime 2 g q8h, pip-tazo 4.5 g q6–8h, or meropenem 1 g q8h). Add vancomycin for line/skin/pneumonia/instability; antifungal if persistent fever.
Dose for the septic pharmacokinetics, not the textbook. Early sepsis expands the volume of distribution (capillary leak, aggressive fluids) and can cause augmented renal clearance, so hydrophilic β-lactams and vancomycin are frequently under-dosed at first — use full loading doses (e.g. vancomycin 25–30 mg/kg) and consider extended/continuous β-lactam infusions to keep drug concentration above the MIC for longer. Later, as AKI develops, the same drugs accumulate and need dose reduction. Re-check renal dosing daily.
Risk factorsMRSA: known colonization/prior MRSA, recent IV antibiotics, hemodialysis, indwelling lines, injection drug use, necrotizing skin infection, post-influenza pneumonia, shock without a source.   Pseudomonas: neutropenia, structural lung disease (bronchiectasis/CF), recent hospitalization/broad-spectrum antibiotics, healthcare-associated infection, prior Pseudomonas.

Source control

Achieve as early as logistically feasible — ideally within 6–12 h: abscess drainage, decompression of an obstructed urinary/biliary system, debridement of necrotizing infection, removal of infected devices/lines. Antibiotics cannot substitute for undrained source control.

Procalcitonin is for stopping, not starting: a falling PCT with clinical improvement supports discontinuation; do not withhold empiric antibiotics because an early PCT is low.

De-escalation, duration & stewardship

  • Reassess at 48–72 h with culture/susceptibility data: stop the anti-MRSA agent if no Gram-positive resistant organism and MRSA nares negative; stop the second antipseudomonal agent; narrow the backbone to the organism identified.
  • Duration: most sepsis with adequate source control needs 7 days (SSC 2021 favors shorter courses). Extend for undrained focus, S. aureus bacteremia (≥14 days, often longer), endocarditis, osteomyelitis, or profound immunocompromise.
  • Procalcitonin can support stopping antibiotics alongside clinical judgment — never to decide whether to start them.
  • IV-to-oral switch once hemodynamically stable, afebrile, tolerating enteral intake, with a susceptible oral option and a controlled source.

Can't-miss source scenarios

ScenarioClueWhat must happen
Necrotizing fasciitisPain out of proportion, rapidly spreading erythema, crepitus, bullae, ↑CK.Emergent surgical debridement + broad antibiotics + clindamycin (antitoxin) — imaging must not delay the OR.
Toxic shock syndromeDiffuse macular rash, desquamation, multi-organ involvement (Strep/Staph toxin).Source removal (tampon, packing), clindamycin/linezolid to suppress toxin, IVIG in severe streptococcal TSS.
Febrile neutropeniaANC <500 with fever; blunted signs.Antipseudomonal β-lactam within 1 h; add vancomycin/antifungal per risk; do not wait for localizing signs.
MeningococcemiaRapidly progressive petechiae/purpura, meningismus.Immediate ceftriaxone (do not delay for LP), droplet precautions, contact prophylaxis.
Obstructive pyelonephritisFlank pain, hydronephrosis, stone.Urgent decompression (stent/nephrostomy) — antibiotics alone fail an obstructed system.
Ascending cholangitisCharcot triad (fever, RUQ pain, jaundice), ↑bili/ALP.Biliary decompression (ERCP) + antibiotics.
Sepsis mimicsNot every shock with fever is septic — consider adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, PE, anaphylaxis, pancreatitis, DKA, toxic ingestions, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Reassess if the patient fails to improve despite appropriate antibiotics and source control.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How common comorbidities change the course & the management

ComorbidityEffect on courseManagement change
CKD / ESRDNephrotoxin sensitivity; limited renal fluid clearance.Renally dose-adjust β-lactams; vancomycin by level. Prefer cefepime + vancomycin over vanc + pip-tazo (less AKI). Fluids still given but reassess frequently for overload.
CHF / low EFPoor tolerance of volume; earlier pulmonary edema.Give the 30 mL/kg bolus but in 250–500 mL aliquots with dynamic reassessment, lung exam, echo; move to vasopressors/inotropes earlier.
CirrhosisHigher baseline lactate (impaired clearance); baseline coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia; ↑infection susceptibility.Interpret lactate trend, not absolute. Consider SBP — paracentesis, ceftriaxone, and albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3 to prevent hepatorenal syndrome.
Immunocompromise / neutropeniaBlunted fever/WBC; atypical & opportunistic pathogens; fulminant course.Broaden empirically (antipseudomonal β-lactam ± vancomycin ± antifungal); lower treatment threshold; febrile neutropenia is an emergency.
Diabetes↑infection risk/severity; DKA/HHS as trigger or complication.Target glucose <180; look for deep/necrotizing infection (foot, emphysematous pyelonephritis); treat ketoacidosis concurrently.
COPDCO₂ retention risk; may already be on steroids.Use the NEWS2 hypercapnic SpO₂ scale; cautious O₂ targets (avoid CO₂ narcosis); permissive hypercapnia if ventilated.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution
  • NSAIDs — worsen AKI and mask fever; avoid in septic AKI.
  • Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam together — synergistic nephrotoxicity; substitute cefepime for pip-tazo when feasible.
  • Aminoglycosides — nephrotoxic; avoid as sole/prolonged therapy in AKI unless resistance demands it.
  • Daptomycin for pneumonia — inactivated by pulmonary surfactant (ineffective).
  • Etomidate for intubation — single dose causes adrenal suppression in septic shock; prefer ketamine.
  • Starch / hydroxyethyl-starch colloids — increased AKI and mortality; do not use.
  • IV sodium bicarbonate for lactic acidosis with pH ≥7.15 solely to improve hemodynamics — no benefit.
  • Dopamine as a routine pressor — more arrhythmias than norepinephrine (SOAP II).
Monitor

Daily trending & fluid responsiveness

📈

What to trend, and how to decide on more fluid

  • Trend daily: lactate clearance, MAP, urine output, mental status, WBC, and (for stewardship) procalcitonin. Reassess antibiotic spectrum against culture data at 48–72 h.
  • Fluid responsiveness — use DYNAMIC measures, de-emphasize static CVP: passive leg raise with stroke-volume/pulse-pressure response, stroke-volume variation / pulse-pressure variation (ventilated, sinus rhythm), IVC collapsibility, or response to a fluid challenge. CVP alone poorly predicts fluid responsiveness.
Sepsis remains a leading cause of inpatient admission and death — early recognition and bundle compliance move outcomes.

Temp > 38 °C or < 36 °C +1
Heart rate > 90 /min +1
RR > 20 /min or PaCO₂ < 32 mmHg +1
WBC > 12k, < 4k, or > 10% bands +1
0 / 4
Select the criteria present.

SIRS is nonspecific (positive in many non-infected patients; ~1 in 8 septic ICU patients are SIRS-negative). Use it as a screen with clinical judgment, not a rule-out.

Escalate

Numeric floor → ICU triggers

⬆️

Concrete thresholds — don't wait for the crash

  • Any new vasopressor requirement, or MAP <65 despite 30 mL/kg fluids.
  • Lactate rising, or failing to clear (<10–20% per 2 h).
  • Escalating oxygen need (e.g. new high-flow/NIV) or RR >30 with distress; PaO₂/FiO₂ <200.
  • Worsening mentation, new arrhythmia/instability, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h despite resuscitation.
  • New AKI with acidosis, hyperkalemia, or volume overload → likely CRRT.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: source controlled; afebrile/hemodynamically stable ≥24 h off pressors; lactate normalized; mentation at baseline; tolerating oral intake; able to complete antibiotics (oral step-down or OPAT arranged); adequate follow-up.

Home

Back to baseline function; reliable oral antibiotics + follow-up.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/therapy or OPAT (IV antibiotics at home).

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing, <3 h therapy/day; ongoing IV antibiotics + deconditioning.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines (post-ICU deconditioning).

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (vent weaning, long IV courses) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Refractory shock/multi-organ failure with goals favoring comfort.
Post-sepsis syndrome is common — cognitive impairment, weakness, and readmission. Arrange early follow-up, medication reconciliation, and rehab; counsel families that recovery takes weeks to months.
🫀 ICU — pressors, steroids, and organ support
Admit

Septic shock — recognition

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Septic shock = sepsis needing vasopressors for MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 despite adequate fluid — hospital mortality >40%. ICU/step-down also for respiratory failure, rapidly progressive multi-organ dysfunction, or refractory acidosis.

Vasoactive escalation in septic shock: fluids → norepinephrine → add fixed-dose vasopressin (± epinephrine) → steroids for refractory shock. Add dobutamine at any point for low cardiac output.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Arterial line for continuous MAP and frequent gases/lactate once on pressors.
  • Central line for vasopressors/high-osmolarity infusions and reliable access — but norepinephrine may run peripherally short-term to avoid delay.
  • Targets: MAP ≥65; lactate clearance (≥10–20%/2 h or normalization); urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; improving mentation; normalizing capillary refill (a validated low-tech perfusion target).
  • De-emphasize static CVP/ScvO₂ mandates — protocolized Rivers-EGDT was no better than good usual care (ProCESS/ARISE/ProMISe).
Phenotype

Hemodynamic phenotypes & echo

🫀

Not all septic shock is the same drip

Bedside echo and the exam sort septic shock into patterns that change the plan. The classic teaching of "warm" vs "cold" shock captures the two ends:

PhenotypeFindingsPhysiologyResponse
Warm (vasodilatory)Bounding pulses, warm flushed skin, wide pulse pressure, brisk cap refill, high/normal CO.Profound NO-driven vasodilation, low SVR — the "classic" early septic picture.Volume + norepinephrine (± vasopressin) to restore SVR.
Cold (hypodynamic)Cool mottled extremities, prolonged cap refill, narrow pulse pressure, low CO; echo shows poor LV function.Sepsis-induced myocardial depression (septic cardiomyopathy) — reversible but real.Norepinephrine to hold MAP + dobutamine for inotropy; reassess volume.
Hypovolemic-dominantCollapsing IVC, high stroke-volume variation, fluid-responsive.Under-resuscitated capillary leak / fluid losses.Further fluids guided by dynamic responsiveness.
Get a bedside echo early in shock that isn't responding as expected: it distinguishes vasodilated-but-hyperdynamic (needs more α tone) from a failing pump (needs an inotrope) from tamponade/RV failure/PE masquerading as sepsis — three completely different treatments.
Peripheral norepinephrine is safe short-termYou do not need to wait for central access to start norepinephrine. A well-sited proximal peripheral IV (AC or above) with monitoring for extravasation is acceptable for the first hours; establish central access when feasible, but never let "no central line" delay a pressor in a crashing patient.
Support

Pressors & inotropes

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose ladder

Norepinephrine — the first-line vasopressor; α1 > β1.
Vaccinationist — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
AgentReceptors / mechanismStart → titrate → maxEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 >> β1~0.05 mcg/kg/min → titrate q5–10 min → practical ceiling ~0.5 (some go higher)↑↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line (SSC 2021, strong).
VasopressinV1 (non-catecholamine)0.03 U/min fixed — do NOT titrate↑SVR; catecholamine-sparingSecond agent — add when norepinephrine reaches ~0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min.
Epinephrineα + β1 + β2~0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min → titrate → ~0.5+↑CO + ↑SVRThird-line add-on; useful with myocardial depression. Watch lactate/tachyarrhythmia.
Angiotensin IIAT1 (renin-angiotensin)Start 20 ng/kg/min per label, titrate↑SVRCatecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock (ATHOS-3: ↑MAP, no mortality benefit).
PhenylephrinePure α1Bolus/infusion↑SVR, reflex ↓HRNiche — tachyarrhythmia limiting norepinephrine, or transient use.
DopamineDose-dependent DA/β/αReservedVariableOnly selected cases (bradycardia, low arrhythmia risk); more arrhythmias — avoid routinely.
Dobutamine (inotrope)β1 > β22.5 mcg/kg/min → titrate → 20 mcg/kg/min↑CO, may ↓SVRAdd for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy / low CO despite adequate MAP + volume.
Norepinephrine's α1 vasoconstriction directly opposes NO-driven vasodilation; vasopressin replaces depleted endogenous AVP and works via V1 when α-receptors are down-regulated — so adding it, rather than pushing norepinephrine ever higher, both raises MAP and spares catecholamine toxicity. Dobutamine's β1 inotropy is reserved for the weak-pump phenotype.
Weight-based vs fixed non-weight-based dosing of norepinephrine both exist (mcg/kg/min vs mcg/min) — know which your unit uses to avoid a 10-fold dosing error.
Adjunct

Corticosteroids & fluids

💊

Refractory-shock adjuncts

1
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day
For norepi/epi ≥0.25 mcg/kg/min for ≥4 h
▾
Treats relative adrenal insufficiency (CIRCI) and restores catecholamine-receptor sensitivity + vascular tone. Give as 50 mg IV q6h or continuous infusion.

Evidence: APROCCHSS (hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone 50 mcg enteral daily) reduced 90-day mortality; ADRENAL (hydrocortisone infusion) sped shock resolution without a mortality benefit. Adding fludrocortisone is reasonable. VITAMINS found the vitamin-C/thiamine/hydrocortisone cocktail no better than hydrocortisone alone — vitamin C is not recommended. Taper steroids once vasopressors are off.

2
Fluids after the initial 30 mL/kg
Guided by dynamic responsiveness, not fixed volumes
▾

Balanced crystalloids preferred over saline (SMART). CLASSIC and CLOVERS found restrictive-fluid/early-pressor strategies no worse than liberal fluids — avoid reflexive large-volume loading. Albumin may be added when large crystalloid volumes are needed (SSC 2021 conditional).

TargetsMAP ≥65 (SEPSISPAM: 80–85 gave no mortality benefit but more AF; higher target reduced RRT in chronic hypertension — individualize upward there). Guide resuscitation to decrease lactate; ANDROMEDA-SHOCK legitimizes capillary-refill-time-targeted resuscitation (non-significantly lower mortality, less organ dysfunction).
Airway

Respiratory support & ventilation

🌬️

Sepsis-associated ARDS — lung-protective settings

Escalate O₂ → high-flow nasal cannula/NIV → intubate for worsening hypoxemia, high work of breathing, or airway/mental-status compromise. For intubation in shock prefer ketamine (avoid etomidate's adrenal suppression) and have a pressor ready for peri-intubation hypotension.

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective (ARDSNet)

< 30 cmH₂O

≥16 h/day for moderate-severe ARDS

Once shock has resolved, adopt a conservative fluid strategy to shorten ventilator days.

Rescue

Other organ support

⚙️

Renal, hematologic, metabolic

  • Renal replacement (CRRT or intermittent HD) for AKI with standard indications (refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, uremia). CRRT preferred when hemodynamically unstable; no benefit to early/prophylactic RRT absent indications.
  • Transfusion threshold Hgb <7 g/dL (TRISS: 7 vs 9 = no mortality difference), target 7–9, barring active ischemia/hemorrhage.
  • Glucose <180 mg/dL (start insulin ~≥180; avoid tight control <110 — hypoglycemia risk).
  • VTE prophylaxis (pharmacologic preferred unless contraindicated); stress-ulcer prophylaxis for ventilation/coagulopathy; early enteral nutrition.
  • Refractory vasodilatory shock: add angiotensin II (ATHOS-3); ensure source control and consider adrenal insufficiency; methylene blue is investigational.
Downgrade

De-escalation to the floor

⬇️

Weaning & downgrade criteria

  • Wean pressors as MAP holds ≥65 with improving perfusion — typically discontinue vasopressin first, then taper norepinephrine (some centers reverse this; watch for rebound hypotension).
  • Taper steroids once vasopressors are off (avoids rebound).
  • Downgrade to floor when: off vasopressors with sustained MAP ≥65 for an appropriate observation window, lactate normalized/normalizing, urine output and mentation improving, stable/declining fluid needs, source controlled, and antibiotics de-escalated/transitioning to oral.
Not yet if… still requiring any vasopressor, lactate not clearing, escalating O₂/ventilatory support, uncontrolled source, or new organ dysfunction. Consider LTAC for prolonged vent weaning, and revisit goals of care in refractory multi-organ failure.
Evidence

Landmark trials

📚

The trials that shaped modern sepsis care

Trial (year)QuestionResultWhy it matters
Kumar (2006)Time-to-antibiotics in septic shock~7.6% ↑ mortality per hour of delayFoundation for early-antibiotic bundles.
ProCESS / ARISE / ProMISe (2014–15)Protocolized EGDT vs usual careNo mortality difference (all three)Ended mandatory Rivers-style CVP/ScvO₂ targets.
SOAP II (2010)Norepinephrine vs dopamineSimilar mortality; dopamine → more arrhythmiasNorepinephrine became first-line.
VASST (2008)Add vasopressin 0.03 U/minNo overall mortality diff; possible benefit in less-severe shockBasis for fixed-dose vasopressin add-on.
SEPSISPAM (2014)MAP 80–85 vs 65–70No mortality diff; more AF high; less RRT in chronic-HTN subgroupSupports MAP ≥65 default.
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019)Capillary-refill vs lactate targetCRT: non-significant ↓ mortality, less organ dysfunctionLegitimizes CRT-guided resuscitation.
ADRENAL (2018)Hydrocortisone infusionFaster shock resolution, no mortality benefitSteroids help hemodynamics.
APROCCHSS (2018)Hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone90-day mortality reductionStrongest steroid mortality signal.
VITAMINS (2020)Vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisoneNo benefit over hydrocortisone aloneKilled the "metabolic cocktail."
CLASSIC (2022) / CLOVERS (2023)Restrictive vs liberal fluidsNo mortality differenceEarly pressors are a safe alternative to more fluid.
SMART (2018)Balanced crystalloid vs salineBenefit favoring balanced (sepsis subgroup ↓ mortality)Prefer balanced crystalloids.
TRISS (2014)Transfusion Hgb 7 vs 9No mortality differenceThreshold Hgb <7.
ATHOS-3 (2017)Angiotensin II in refractory shock↑MAP response (69.9% vs 23.4%), no mortality benefitRescue vasopressor option.
Twelve high-yield truths: (1) antibiotics ≤1 h; (2) cultures before — never delaying — antibiotics; (3) track lactate clearance; (4) EGDT is dead; (5) dynamic > static (CVP) fluid assessment; (6) balanced crystalloid > saline; (7) norepinephrine first, dopamine causes arrhythmias; (8) add fixed vasopressin rather than sky-high norepinephrine; (9) MAP ≥65 default; (10) steroids for refractory shock, fludrocortisone adds a mortality signal, vitamin C does not work; (11) procalcitonin for stopping not starting; (12) source control is non-negotiable.
